cleanIntro: The 1911-380 is a scaled 1911: recoil-operated, tilting barrel, locked breech, single action, with an ambidextrous thumb "safety", a grip "safety", a magazine "safety" and an eight-round magazine of .380 ACP. Its field strip is the classic 1911 sequence — bushing, plug, slide stop, slide, spring, barrel — and it ends there by instruction. ⛔ Read this first: ONE Browning manual covers BOTH the 1911-380 and the 1911-22, and the two pistols are mechanically different guns. The 1911-22 is a straight blow-back rimfire; several of the warnings printed in that book name the 1911-22 by model and are NOT statements about your .380. Every one of them is surfaced below with its model attached, so you can see which side of the line it sits on rather than reading a rimfire instruction onto a centrefire pistol.

steps.title: One manual, two mechanically different pistols
steps.action: Establish which pistol you are holding before you follow any instruction in this book, because Browning covers two guns in it and they are not variants of each other. The 1911-380 is recoil-operated with a tilting barrel and a locked breech — the barrel unlocks from the slide as it moves back, exactly like a full-size 1911. The 1911-22 is a straight blow-back with a fixed barrel and no locking at all. The field strip below is shared, but any statement in the manual that names a model applies only to that model, and this guide flags each one.
steps.prose: The serial number is stamped on the right side of the frame above the trigger guard, and the calibre is inscribed on the right side of the barrel.
steps.caution: Model-named warnings in this manual bind that model only. Check which pistol yours is.
steps.quote: The Browning 1911-22 is a recoil-operated, straight-blowback, single-action autoloading pistol. The Browning 1911-380 is a recoil-operated, tilting barrel, locked-breech, single-action autoloading pistol.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — General Description and Operation

steps.title: 380 ACP only — and read the barrel inscription to confirm it
steps.action: This is the ammunition statement that belongs to your pistol. Browning chambers 1911-380 pistols for 380 ACP cartridges only, and directs you to the inscription on the right side of the barrel as the record on your individual gun. Examine every cartridge as it goes into the magazine rather than trusting the box: .380 ACP sits close enough to several other small automatic-pistol cartridges that a stray round can look right in a hand. The 1911-380 is a locked-breech pistol whose timing depends on that specific pressure curve, so a wrong cartridge does not simply function badly, it functions unpredictably.
steps.prose: Magazine capacity on the 1911-380 is eight rounds of 380 ACP.
steps.quote: WARNING: BROWNING 1911-380 PISTOLS ARE CHAMBERED FOR 380 ACP CARTRIDGES ONLY. DO NOT USE AMMUNITION OTHER THAN WHAT IS INSCRIBED ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE BARREL.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Ammunition

steps.title: The 22 Long Rifle warning on the same page is the 1911-22's, not yours
steps.action: Immediately above the 380 statement, the same page carries a warning that reads exactly the same way but names a different pistol and a different cartridge. It is printed there because this one book serves both guns, and it is not an alternative loading for a 1911-380 — a .22 LR round in a .380 chamber has no case support at all and the pistol is not built to fire it. Read which model a warning names before you act on it. The tell is easy on this page: two warnings, identical wording, different model and different cartridge.
steps.prose: This is the exact substitution hazard that comes with a shared manual, and Browning's own layout is what invites it.
steps.caution: This warning names the 1911-22. Your 1911-380 takes 380 ACP.
steps.quote: WARNING: BROWNING 1911-22 PISTOLS ARE CHAMBERED FOR 22 LONG RIFLE CARTRIDGES ONLY. DO NOT USE AMMUNITION OTHER THAN WHAT IS INSCRIBED ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE BARREL.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Ammunition (1911-22 statement, printed beside the 1911-380 statement)

steps.title: The 22 Short / 22 Long / blanks prohibition is also a 1911-22 statement
steps.action: There is a second rimfire-specific NOTICE further down the ammunition page and it belongs to the 1911-22 as well. It bars 22 Short, 22 Long and blanks from the rimfire pistol because all three share the .22 rim and will chamber in it. None of those cartridges have any bearing on a 1911-380 — they will not chamber in a .380 barrel — so the practical point for a 1911-380 owner is simply that this NOTICE is not about your gun and its silence about .380 loads is not permission for anything. Your limit is the one printed with your model's name on it.
steps.prose: Always read the ammunition label and any enclosures with the ammunition to be sure there is no restriction on its use with your firearm.
steps.caution: A 1911-22 restriction. It does not describe what a 1911-380 may be fed.
steps.quote: NOTICE: BROWNING 1911-22 PISTOLS MUST BE USED WITH ONLY 22 LONG RIFLE RIMFIRE AMMUNITION AS DESIGNATED ON THE BARREL. DO NOT SHOOT 22 SHORT OR 22 LONG AMMUNITION OR BLANKS.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Ammunition (1911-22 statement)

steps.title: The dry-fire NOTICE names the 1911-22 — and rule 15 still covers you
steps.action: The dry-firing prohibition printed twice in this manual names the 1911-22 pistol specifically, which is the model with a rimfire firing pin that strikes the chamber mouth on an empty chamber. Browning prints no equivalent model-named notice for the 1911-380, and it is not this guide's job to invent one. What does bind every pistol in the book is the manual's own safety rule 15, which says not to snap the firing pin on an empty chamber because the chamber may not be empty. If you intend to practise the trigger on a 1911-380, unload it completely, check the chamber, and treat the snap as the safety question rather than the mechanical one.
steps.prose: Note also that on either pistol the magazine "safety" means the trigger will not operate the hammer at all unless a magazine is inserted.
steps.caution: This dry-fire NOTICE is written against the 1911-22. No model-named equivalent is printed for the 1911-380.
steps.quote: NOTICE: DO NOT DRY FIRE THE 1911-22 PISTOL. DRY FIRING MAY DAMAGE THE FIREARM COMPONENTS, POSSIBLY RENDERING THE FIREARM INOPERABLE.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — General Description and Operation (repeated verbatim under the "Dry Firing" heading)

steps.title: Which safeties your pistol has — the 1911-22 Al is the odd one out
steps.action: Three "safeties" are in play on a 1911-380: an ambidextrous manual thumb "safety" workable from either side, a grip "safety" on the upper rear of the grip, and a magazine "safety" that stops the trigger from operating the hammer unless a magazine is inserted. The manual separates that from the 1911-22 Al, which has a single left-side thumb "safety" rather than an ambidextrous one — so a paragraph describing a left-side-only lever is not describing your pistol. For the 1911-380 to fire, the thumb "safety" must be off safe AND the grip "safety" fully depressed by a normal firing grip. The thumb lever also cannot be pushed up to on safe unless the hammer is at full cock.
steps.prose: Use only an UNLOADED magazine when you need to disengage the magazine "safety" for hammer lowering or a function check.
steps.caution: The left-side-only thumb safety describes the 1911-22 Al. The 1911-380's is ambidextrous.
steps.quote: Browning 1911-22 Al pistols feature a manual thumb "safety" located on the left side of the firearm and a grip "safety" located on the upper rear portion of the pistol grip.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — "SAFETY" MECHANISM (1911-22 Al statement; the following sentence covers 1911-22 and 1911-380 as ambidextrous)

steps.title: Magazine out first — the magazine safety is not proof of anything
steps.action: Press the magazine release on the left side of the frame at the rear of the trigger guard and draw the magazine out. With it gone the magazine "safety" blocks the trigger, and that is precisely why it must not be mistaken for an unloaded gun: the trigger is dead and a .380 round can still be in the chamber. Browning prints the correction in the same sentence as the instruction. Count the rounds that come out against the eight the 1911-380's magazine holds, and set it aside.
steps.prose: Keep the muzzle in a safe direction throughout; nothing has been proved yet.
steps.quote: 1. Press the magazine release and remove the magazine. Remember, merely removing the magazine does not mean the chamber is unloaded.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Unloading > UNLOADING THE PISTOL, step 1
steps.warn: A blocked trigger is the magazine safety, not an empty chamber.

steps.title: Slide back, eject, lock it open on the slide stop, then look
steps.action: Put the thumb "safety" into the off safe position — the lever cannot come off the slide recess with the hammer down, and the slide will not run with the safety up — then grasp the rear slide serrations, draw the slide fully back to eject the chambered round, and push the slide stop up into the recess in the slide to hold it open. Look into the chamber and the ejection port and confirm nothing is there. On the 1911-380 the barrel tilts as the slide comes back, so the chamber is visible through the port at the top of the barrel, not down the frame rails.
steps.prose: With no magazine inserted the slide stop has to be pushed up by hand; it only self-engages off an empty magazine.
steps.quote: 3. Pull back on the slide and eject the cartridge in the chamber. Lock the slide to the rear by sliding the slide stop up. Inspect the chamber to ensure no cartridge is present.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Unloading > UNLOADING THE PISTOL, step 3
steps.warn: Keep fingers out of the ejection port; the slide closes hard under spring pressure.

steps.title: Empty the magazine itself and any spares
steps.action: The 1911-380 magazine holds its rounds under feed lips and will not tip out. Push forward on the rim of the top cartridge and slide it out, letting the follower carry the next one up, and repeat until the body is empty — eight at most on this model. Work forward on the rim rather than levering upward on the case mouth, which is how a .380 round gets its bullet set back. Do every spare magazine on the bench at the same time, then move all ammunition out of the cleaning area entirely.
steps.prose: One unloaded magazine stays with the pistol: you need it inserted to work the hammer past the magazine "safety".
steps.quote: 3. Strip the cartridges from the magazine by pushing forward on the rim of the top cartridge and sliding each cartridge out, one at a time, as each moves up in the magazine.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Unloading > UNLOADING THE MAGAZINE, step 3

steps.title: Set the pistol up — unloaded, slide forward, rear end braced
steps.action: Browning's disassembly opens with the magazine out, the "safety" in the OFF safe position, the chamber visually checked and the slide returned forward. Then rest the rear of the pistol on a firm, no-slip surface. That bracing matters more than it looks: the next move needs one hand pressing a compressed recoil spring down into the slide while the other rotates the bushing, and a pistol sliding around under that hand is how the plug launches. Put eye protection on now — the recoil spring and plug are under tension for the whole of the next two steps.
steps.prose: For the takedown the manual has you replace an unloaded magazine and lower the hammer to the dropped position beforehand.
steps.quote: 4. Rest the rear of the pistol on a firm, no-slip surface (Figure 17).
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Disassembly, step 4
steps.warn: Eye protection from here on — the recoil spring and plug are spring-tensioned.

steps.title: Plug down, bushing clockwise 90°, then let the spring out under control
steps.action: Press and hold the recoil spring plug down into the slide with your thumb, then rotate the barrel bushing clockwise 90 degrees so its lugs no longer trap the plug. Keep the plug captive under your thumb while it turns — the recoil spring is compressed behind it, and this is the moment the plug becomes free. Now release the tension slowly and lift the plug out. On a 1911-380 the parts are lighter and shorter than a full-size 1911's but the spring is still doing real work, and a plug let go at speed goes across the room and is not always found.
steps.prose: Note the direction: clockwise 90° to release. The bushing goes counterclockwise 90° at the end of reassembly to lock the plug back in.
steps.quote: 5. Press and hold the recoil spring plug down into the slide and rotate the barrel bushing clockwise 90° (Figure 18).
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Disassembly, step 5
steps.warn: Never let the recoil spring plug fly. Release the tension under thumb control.

steps.title: Line up the disassembly recess and drive the slide stop out
steps.action: Ease the slide rearward until the disassembly recess in its lower edge sits over the slide stop — there is a distinct notch, and the slide stop will not come out at any other position because the stop's shaft passes through the barrel link. Then push on the protruding end of the slide stop shaft from the RIGHT side of the frame and pull the stop out from the LEFT. Do not lever it out with a screwdriver; the tool marks land on the frame right where they show. If the stop will not move, the recess is not aligned, not the stop being tight.
steps.prose: The slide stop's shaft is also what holds the barrel link, which is why the barrel comes out later rather than now.
steps.quote: 7. Move the slide rearward until the disassembly recess aligns with the slide stop. 8. Press the protruding part of the slide stop shaft through the right side of the frame. Grasp the slide stop and pull it from the left side of the frame (Figure 20).
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Disassembly, steps 7-8

steps.title: Slide forward off the frame, then the spring and guide rod out
steps.action: With the slide stop out, run the slide forward and straight off the front of the frame rails. Then take the recoil spring out through the front of the slide and lift the recoil spring guide rod off the barrel block. Note the guide rod's orientation as it comes away — it has a notched side that faces the barrel on reassembly and a tab that has to sit into the barrel block, and it is easy to put back reversed. The slide is now off and the frame keeps the hammer, sear and both frame-mounted safeties, none of which you are going to touch.
steps.prose: Keep the spring, plug and guide rod together as a set; the plug is the one that goes missing.
steps.quote: 9. Pull the slide forward and off the frame (Figure 21). 10. Remove the recoil spring through the front of the slide. Lift the recoil spring guide rod from the barrel block (Figure 22).
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Disassembly, steps 9-10

steps.title: Bushing out, then the barrel forward out of the slide
steps.action: Rotate the barrel bushing counterclockwise about 45 degrees, until its lugs line up with the opening in the front of the slide, and lift it clear. With the bushing gone the muzzle end of the barrel is no longer captured, so the barrel slides out through the front of the slide. On the 1911-380 the barrel is a tilting, locked-breech barrel with locking lugs on top and a link underneath — handle it by the block rather than the lugs, and put it down where the lug faces cannot get knocked against anything hard. That is the strip complete.
steps.prose: Bushing rotation is 90° at the plug stage and roughly 45° here. Two different rotations on the same part.
steps.quote: 11. Rotate the barrel bushing counterclockwise approximately 45° until the barrel bushing lugs align with the opening in the front of the slide and remove the barrel bushing (Figure 23). 12. Slide the barrel through the front of the slide (Figure 24).
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Disassembly, steps 11-12

steps.title: That is enough — the pistol is stripped for normal maintenance
steps.action: Stop here. Browning states in as many words that no further disassembly is recommended because the pistol is now stripped adequately for normal maintenance and cleaning. Everything the cleaning procedure asks you to reach is now reachable: the bore and chamber from the breech end, the breech face and extractor, the frame rails, the barrel's locking lugs and the feed ramp. There is no reason to go into the frame for grip screws, mainspring housing, sear or firing pin, and no procedure published for putting any of it back.
steps.prose: The manual shows the finished state in Figure 25 for the 1911-22 and Figure 26 for the 1911-380 — check yours against the right figure.
steps.quote: No further disassembly is recommended as the pistol is now stripped adequately for normal maintenance and cleaning.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Disassembly, after step 12
steps.warn: This is the full published strip. Nothing beyond it is sanctioned.

steps.title: Anything deeper is Browning's own service facility, not a gunsmith's choice
steps.action: Browning's boundary on this pistol is unusually firm and worth reading exactly. If further disassembly ever becomes necessary it is to be performed only by the Browning service facility in Arnold, Missouri or an authorised Browning service centre, and no other person should attempt further disassembly or reassembly procedures. The reason given is reassembly, not teardown: incorrect reassembly could render the firearm inoperative or unsafe, which on a locked-breech pistol with a grip safety and a magazine safety means a gun that looks normal and behaves unpredictably. Send it rather than open it.
steps.prose: Return it unloaded, with optics and accessories removed, packed securely, and never with ammunition in the box.
steps.quote: IF FURTHER DISASSEMBLY SHOULD EVER BECOME NECESSARY IT SHOULD ONLY BE PERFORMED BY OUR SERVICE FACILITY IN ARNOLD, MISSOURI, OR AN AUTHORIZED BROWNING SERVICE CENTER. NO OTHER PERSON SHOULD ATTEMPT TO PERFORM FURTHER DISASSEMBLY/REASSEMBLY PROCEDURES.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Disassembly, closing notice
steps.warn: Further disassembly: Browning service only. Not a gunsmith, not you.

steps.title: Bore — a 35 calibre / 9mm jag for the 1911-380, not a 22
steps.action: This is the one place the cleaning procedure splits by model, so get the right tooling. Browning specifies a 22 calibre slotted tip or jag for 1911-22 models and a 35 calibre / 9mm slotted tip or jag for 1911-380 models, sized to give a snug fit in the bore. A .22 jag in a .380 barrel does not clean it — it rattles through, wets the bore and leaves the fouling exactly where it was, while telling you the job is done. With the barrel out, run the rod in at the breech end and back and forth several times, keeping the rod clear of the muzzle crown.
steps.prose: Normal powder residue is expected and not serious; a nitro-solvent patch usually lifts it. Use a bronze brush only when fouling is heavy, pushed fully through before withdrawing.
steps.caution: 1911-380 takes a 35 calibre / 9mm jag. The 22 jag in the same sentence is the 1911-22's.
steps.quote: Clean the bore using a pistol cleaning rod with a 22 caliber slotted tip or cleaning jag and patch for 1911-22 models or a 35 caliber/9mm slotted tip or cleaning jag and patch for 1911-380 models, to provide a snug fit in the bore.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, step 2

steps.title: Copper solvent after copper-plated bullets
steps.action: Plated .380 practice ammunition leaves copper in the bore that nitro solvent does not remove, and it plates on rather than sitting loose. Browning's instruction is a quality copper solvent, swabbed through to the solvent maker's own procedure, after shooting copper-plated bullets — and it notes that this residue needs cleaning more often than powder fouling does. Follow the solvent's dwell time rather than scrubbing hard, then wipe the chamber and bore dry and pass one lightly oiled patch through for preservation. Check afterwards that no patch has been left in the barrel or chamber.
steps.prose: Solvents are highly flammable and most are unkind to a pistol's finish — keep them off the outside of the slide and wear eye protection.
steps.quote: To maintain the utmost accuracy of your pistol it is recommended you clean the bore with a quality copper solvent after shooting copper-plated bullets.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, step 2

steps.title: Oil the named points lightly — too much is a malfunction
steps.action: Brush or wipe the dirt out of the slide and the rest of the action first, then put a light film of quality light gun oil on the lubrication points Browning illustrates: the frame rails, the barrel's bearing surfaces and the slide's interior contact areas. Use it sparingly. Excessive lubricant on a small locked-breech pistol interferes with function — it collects unburnt powder into a paste in the rails and slows the slide exactly when the .380's modest impulse needs it free. Light oils also evaporate, so re-lubricate a 1911-380 that has been stored for any length of time before shooting it.
steps.prose: Wipe every exposed metal surface with a lightly oiled cloth afterwards and take the finger marks off; they are where moisture sits.
steps.caution: A light film only. Re-oil after storage — light oils evaporate.
steps.quote: NOTICE: DO NOT USE EXCESSIVE LUBRICANT. USING TOO MUCH LUBRICANT CAN INTERFERE WITH THE FUNCTION OF YOUR PISTOL.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES

steps.title: The magazine is flushed, not opened
steps.action: Clean the 1911-380 magazine as an assembled unit: spray it inside and out with an aerosol solvent that will not attack the polymer follower or corrode the metal, cycle the follower to break the dirt loose, then depress the follower and run a rod with a tip and patch into the top to clear the built-up deposit at the front of the body. Spray it again, shake out the excess and dry it with a cloth or compressed air. Browning's interval is by round count — normally after 500 to 1000 cartridges — and by inspection whenever the follower feels gritty.
steps.prose: Let it dry fully before it goes back in the pistol; solvent left in a magazine ends up on the ammunition.
steps.quote: Frequently inspect magazines to determine the need for cleaning as lubricant and dirt will gradually collect in the mechanism. Normally, the magazine should be cleaned after firing 500 to 1000 cartridges.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING THE MAGAZINE

steps.title: Never further apart than the manual explains
steps.action: The closing notice bounds the whole book rather than any one procedure: never take the firearm apart further than the manual explains, because it is a specialized, finely fitted mechanism and disassembling the inner mechanism assemblies may permanently damage it. On a 1911-380 the inner mechanism means everything left in the frame — hammer, sear, disconnector, the grip safety and the magazine safety — plus the extractor and firing pin still in the slide. Where further disassembly is genuinely needed for service or cleaning, it goes to a qualified gunsmith or to the Arnold, Missouri facility.
steps.prose: A pistol dropped in water is the classic case where this applies immediately rather than eventually.
steps.quote: NOTICE: NEVER ATTEMPT TO TAKE YOUR FIREARM APART FURTHER THAN EXPLAINED IN THIS OWNER’S MANUAL. YOUR FIREARM IS A SPECIALIZED, FINELY FITTED MECHANISM. YOU MAY PERMANENTLY DAMAGE IT BY ATTEMPTING TO DISASSEMBLE THE INNER MECHANISM ASSEMBLIES.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING THE MAGAZINE, closing notice

steps.title: Field strip complete
steps.action: Six pieces should be in front of you: frame, slide, barrel, barrel bushing, recoil spring with its guide rod, and the recoil spring plug — plus the empty magazine. Nothing else on a 1911-380 comes off, and Browning shows the finished state in Figure 26 specifically (Figure 25 is the 1911-22, so compare against the right one). Clean it after every day of shooting and more often if it gets excessively dirty; a minimum session is wiping down the action and oiling the key parts. If a function problem survives a thorough clean, that is when it goes to Browning rather than further apart.
steps.prose: Reassembly runs the sequence backwards with two traps: the guide rod goes in notched side toward the barrel, and the bushing turns counterclockwise 90° to lock the plug at the end.
steps.quote: Clean your pistol after every day of shooting, and more often if it becomes excessively dirty. A minimum cleaning includes wiping down the action and oiling key parts. Most regular maintenance will also include cleaning the barrel.
steps.cite: 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES

deepAbsentReason: The 1911-22 and 1911-380 Owner's Manual publishes the twelve-step field strip walked above — magazine, chamber check, plug and bushing, slide stop, slide, recoil spring and guide rod, bushing, barrel — and then STOPS, in its own words. Immediately after step 12 Browning states that no further disassembly is recommended because the pistol is now stripped adequately for normal maintenance and cleaning, and the closing notice of the Disassembly section goes further than most Browning books: if further disassembly should ever become necessary it should only be performed by the Browning service facility in Arnold, Missouri or an authorised Browning service centre, and NO OTHER PERSON should attempt further disassembly or reassembly, because incorrect reassembly could render the firearm inoperative or unsafe. Nothing is published for the frame group (hammer, sear, disconnector, grip "safety", magazine "safety", mainspring housing, grip panels) or for the slide's internals (firing pin, firing pin spring, extractor). The magazine is cleaned assembled by spraying, cycling and drying, with no disassembly given. The cleaning section closes with the standing notice never to take the firearm apart further than the manual explains. There is therefore no deeper published procedure for a 1911-380, and none has been invented.

cleaning.name: BARREL, BORE & CHAMBER (barrel out of the slide)
tasks: 35 calibre / 9mm slotted tip or jag and patch for a 1911-380 — NOT the 22 jag specified for 1911-22 models
Rod entered at the breech end, run back and forth several times
Keep the rod off the muzzle crown — damage there costs accuracy permanently
Bronze bore brush with nitro solvent only when fouling is heavy; push fully through before withdrawing
Quality copper solvent after shooting copper-plated bullets, to the solvent maker's procedure
Clean the locking lugs on top of the barrel and the feed ramp at the breech
Wipe dry, one lightly oiled patch, then confirm no patch was left in the barrel or chamber

cleaning.name: SLIDE & FRAME
tasks: Small brush or rag to lift dirt and foreign matter from the slide and the rest of the action
Scrub the breech face and the extractor cut where the case head rides
Clean the frame rails and the slide's interior bearing surfaces
Light film of quality light gun oil at the illustrated lubrication points — sparingly
DO NOT use excessive lubricant; it interferes with the function of the pistol
Light oils evaporate — re-lubricate before shooting a pistol that has been stored

cleaning.name: RECOIL ASSEMBLY & BUSHING
tasks: Wipe the recoil spring, guide rod and plug; note the guide rod's notched side and tab
Clean inside the barrel bushing where it bears on the barrel
Keep spring, guide rod and plug together as one set
Eye protection whenever the spring and plug are under tension

cleaning.name: MAGAZINE (assembled — never opened)
tasks: Normally cleaned after 500 to 1000 cartridges, or when inspection shows build-up
Aerosol solvent safe for the polymer follower and non-corrosive to the metal, inside and out
Cycle the follower to loosen dirt and grease
Depress the follower and run a rod tip and patch into the top to clear deposits at the front
Shake out the excess and dry with a cloth or compressed air

reassembly: Replace the barrel into the slide from the front.
Align the barrel bushing lugs with the spring opening in the slide, fit the bushing, and rotate it clockwise so it clears the recoil spring.
Replace the recoil spring guide NOTCHED SIDE TOWARD THE BARREL: slide it into the forward part of the slide, then rearward into the barrel block, and make sure the tab seats into the block.
Insert the recoil spring through the front of the slide and over the guide, then fit the recoil spring plug.
Lightly compress the plug to hold it in place, put the slide back on the frame, and move the slide rearward until the disassembly notch lines up with the slide stop opening.
Replace the slide stop in the frame from the left.
Press the recoil spring plug into the slide and rotate the barrel bushing COUNTERCLOCKWISE 90° until the plug locks into position.
Insert a completely unloaded magazine and lower the hammer to the dropped position.
Eye protection stays on for the plug and bushing steps — the spring is under tension in both directions.
fncheck: Look through the bore against a light and confirm it is clear and that no patch remains in the barrel or chamber. With the pistol unloaded and an EMPTY magazine inserted, cycle the slide by hand several times and confirm it runs freely, locks back on the slide stop when the stop is pushed up, and closes cleanly when it is pressed down. Confirm the barrel bushing is locked by the recoil spring plug and cannot be turned by hand. Confirm the thumb "safety" pushes up into the slide recess only with the hammer at full cock, and that it works from both sides — the 1911-380's is ambidextrous. Confirm the grip "safety" blocks the trigger until a normal firing grip depresses it, and that with no magazine inserted the trigger will not operate the hammer at all. Check the slide stop is fully seated and its shaft flush on the right side of the frame. Never test the mechanical function of the pistol with live ammunition, and keep all ammunition out of the cleaning area.
